text.en: In the 1000s Guido of Arezzo set staff lines a third apart, so lines and spaces each hold a note, and coloured two lines red and yellow. Chant books still use his four lines.

source.en: Encyclopedia.com, Guido of Arezzo (New Catholic Encyclopedia)

headline.en: A stave is five lines. Every line and every space is one note, and higher on the stave is higher in pitch. Your do sits where your own note is.

Early Western chant notation, from the 800s, had no staff. Its marks showed a tune's general rise and fall, not its exact notes, probably as reminders of melodies singers had already learned by ear.

headline.en: A step goes from a line to the next space, or a space to the next line. Up the stave is up in pitch.

Taps, the US Army's lights-out call, was reworked from an older bugle call in July 1862. A bugle plays only its harmonic series, so Taps uses just one major chord: so, do and mi.

headline.en: Do, mi and so are the notes of your home chord. On the stave each sits two steps above the last: line to line, or space to space.

Old music printers disliked ledger lines: hard to set in type, wasteful of space and messy-looking. Vocal music instead used many different clefs to keep each part on the stave as much as possible.

headline.en: Many tunes start below do, on the so beneath it, and leap up home. On the stave it's a skip and a step lower.

The minim's Latin name, minima, means "smallest": it was once the shortest note value. And the breve, now worth two semibreves, was named from the Latin for "short", the root of "brief".

headline.en: Now the notes' shapes tell you how long. A filled note with a stem is one beat; a hollow one with a stem is two. A rest is silence that still counts: this one, a beat.

text.en: Vocal scores traditionally beamed quavers only when they shared one syllable, so each new syllable got its own flag. Today it's more common to beam by the beat and show shared syllables with slurs.

headline.en: A quaver is half a beat. It has a flag, or it's joined to its neighbour by a beam, and two fit in one beat.

text.en: Elizabethan English singers used just four syllables, mi, fa, sol and la, singing fa, sol, la twice to fill a scale. In King Lear's 1623 Folio, Edmund adds "Fa, sol, la, me."

headline.en: La is a step above so: on the stave, the next line or space up. There's a low la too, a skip below do, just above low so.

Kodály educators found children struggled to sing half steps in tune. So the method starts with mi and so, adds la, do and re, and brings in fa and ti only once those feel comfortable.

headline.en: Ti sits just below do. Mi to fa and ti to do look like every other step on the stave, but they're half as far: sing them close.

In shape-note singing each syllable has its own note-head shape, and a minor key's first note is always la, as yours is now. Little and Smith printed the shapes in 1801.

text.en: Sharps in a key signature always come in the same order, F, C, G, D, A, E, B, and flats in the reverse order. Each new key a fifth higher adds the next sharp.

source.en: Wikipedia, "Key signature" (citing George Thaddeus Jones, Music Theory, 1974)

headline.en: Real music starts each line with a key signature: the sharps or flats there say which notes are always raised or lowered. Do moves with the key: it's the key's home note.

text.en: Medieval and Renaissance church choirs sang from choirbooks big enough for all to read, each part on its own patch of the open pages. The book sat on a stand: boys in front, men behind.
